newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Africans focus on sound management for growth.
newsitem.headline: Africans focus on sound management for growth.

text.p: African finance ministers on Thursday called for economic reforms to achieve sustainable growth, integration in the world economy and reduced dependence on foreign financing.

The ministers urged Africans to adopt globally accepted practises in managing banks, to improve mobilisation of domestic savings, to speed up privatisations and to strengthen or establish stock exchanges.
On Wednesday the ministers ended a three-day conference in the Ethiopian capital called by the U.N. Economic Commission for Africa and focussed on debt and financial reforms.
"The ministers call upon African countries to implement appropriate measures to reduce gradually their heavy dependency on external financing," a statement at the end of the conference said.

The African ministers committed themselves to economic reforms and enhancing debt and macroeconomic management capabilities, but also asked the Paris Club of bilateral creditors to take effective measures to reduce debt.

They urged multilateral financial institutions to support Africa with concessionary financing, including grants, to enable faster social development and rehabilitation of health, education and general infrastructures.
One of the meeting's concerns was a World Bank and International Monetary Fund-led debt relief initiative roundly criticised for its rigid eligibility criteria.

"We continue to be concerned that the magnitudes of the debt are obviously unsustainable. This initiative is a partial reflection of the commitment of the global community to finding a lasting solution to the problem," the ministers said.

Africa's debt stock was estimated at $340.5 billion at the end of 1996 and total debt service payments amounted to $24 billion. African ministers said in extreme cases, some countries spent 90 percent of all revenues on debt servicing.

"Liberalised macroeconomic policies and political reforms currently being implemented in Africa are intended to provide the necessary environment conducive to both local and foreign investment. We commit ourselves to continuing these reforms and urge the donor community to support our efforts," the ministers said.

They called for specific measures to make central banks autonomous, systematic restructuring of banking concerns to encourage efficiency, the removal of credit market segmentation to enhance competition and the liberalisation of interest rates.
The ministers called for a move towards liberalised currencies for countries not yet on that path and bolstering of regional economic groupings as a launch pad for growth.

"We cannot create integration such as the European Union. We are at very different levels of development. But in regional groups we can share our experiences and help each other along," Chris Stals, Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, told Reuters. "With other reforms, that's a way forward."

"African countries must fully accept to carry the principal responsibility of raising resources to develop their countries. They must improve tax collection, strengthen the finances of public utilities and apply austerity in use of public funds," said Zambian Finance Minister Ronald Penza.

"The achievement of genuine self-reliant export-oriented economic growth will be the end result of our combined efforts," added Penza, whose country has become a leading economic reform pupil and is registering impressive growth.
